subject: Just a nice figure for intuitively explaining HMC to students

messages.author: f769d7d2cfcf4edc
messages.subject: Just a nice figure for intuitively explaining HMC to students
parts:
Hey everyone,

I was playing with rgl and thought others might appreciate this figure I generated for explaining what an HMC sampler is more or less doing.
I actually generated it for a class paper because the prof is not familiar with Bayesian inference, posterior distributions, MCMC, or HMC.

I more or less explain it as "imagine flipping this upside down and rolling a ball around in it and recording the coordinates in space every so many seconds.
The samples were from stan, of course, using NUTS. Though the image isn't on the log-scale, I still tell the students (or the prof) to flip it upside down and imagine randomly flicking a marble in some direction and recording the positions.
This made sense to many of my undergraduates, and they better understood what I meant by a marginal distribution too. The inner line is the first 10 non-warmup steps.

The figure is below, but one can view a webGL version of it (that you can rotate and such) in the attached index.html.

ShinyStan can automatically generate those plots for arbitrary models
and it lets you rotate them with up to three parameters.

The trick is explaining why you get a bowl in the first place (conserved
Hamiltonian gives you a level set).

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Just a nice figure for intuitively explaining HMC to students
parts:
I thought Jonah showed me that ShinyStan could do what you
were doing. But apparently not, because they added an issue to
add the feature. So it will be able to do it soon. There's something
at least in 2D that will plot trajectories, but they quickly become
very hard to scan without thinning, which kind of defeats the purpose.

The really cool trajectories to visualize (though it's HMC specific)
is the Hamiltonian simulation within an iteration. Right now there's
a problem that we see where a divergent transition started, but not
where it gets into trouble.

- Bob

messages.author: 395bdca538bcae5d
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Just a nice figure for intuitively explaining HMC to students
parts: I agree with Bob about showing within iteration steps. In my experience trying to explain HMC to people people aren't used to thinking about joint posteriors, particularly in >3 dimensions (they tend to only think of marginals). Thus an illustrative 2d example is much more intuitive to people. That's why I made Figure 3b in my paper (here), which shows three trajectories: unit diagonal mass matrix, dense mass matrix, and divergence. -Cole

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Just a nice figure for intuitively explaining HMC to students
parts:
Hi all,

Cole and Stephen, these figures are great!  Thank you for sharing here.

In case it's useful to anyone, allow me to also throw in a simple animation of a sequence of HMC trajectories around a 2D gaussian that I made a few years ago for illustrative purposes in talks.  An mp4 video, still frames, and python/matplotlib code to generate the animation are here -

https://github.com/nesanders/HMC_viz

The final frame shows a marginal view by rotating the Gaussian to a 2D perspective.  Stephen, I really like your marginal views on the side of the box.

~Nathan

parts:
Is there interest from the Stan team for pulling illustrative/informative figures together more formally? For instance, should the Stan manual have some figures trying to explain what NUTS trajectory is? I've thought a lot about explaining this to new HMC users, and have some additional ideas for good figs.

Is that something that would be worth adding to the Stan manual. Or is there another place? 

Realistically that would be the only way I could contribute back to the Stan project (and maybe others too).
